segments.text: Episode sixty-one. Season four: extremes. Next stop... the coldest place in the universe.
Space is cold. Even empty space, far from any star, has a temperature of about minus two hundred seventy degrees Celsius.
segments.headline: Empty space is cold

segments.text: That warmth, just under three degrees above absolute zero, comes from the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.
But about five thousand light-years away, in the constellation Centaurus, there's a place even colder. The Boomerang Nebula.
segments.headline: The Boomerang Nebula

segments.text: It's about one degree above absolute zero. Minus two hundred seventy-two degrees Celsius.
It's the coldest natural place known in the universe. Colder than empty space itself.
segments.headline: Colder than space

segments.text: How? A dying star at its center is blowing out gas extremely fast, at more than a hundred and fifty kilometers per second.
segments.headline: A dying star

segments.text: When gas expands that quickly, it cools down. It's the same reason a spray can gets cold in your hand.
segments.headline: Like a spray can

segments.text: The only colder places we know are in laboratories on Earth, where scientists cool atoms to within a billionth of a degree of absolute zero.
segments.headline: Colder only in labs

segments.text: Tomorrow, the opposite extreme. Temperatures of trillions of degrees. Next stop: the hottest places in the universe. Follow, so you don't miss episode sixty-two.
